title: Twin Flames Universe.com, Inc. v. Cole
lead: A Michigan online business sued an Arizona critic over worldwide posts and an interview, but the court found no Michigan-directed conduct and declined a transfer after examining the plaintiffs’ threats.

actors.name: Twin Flames Universe and the Ayans
actors.role: Michigan-based plaintiffs alleging defamation and interference

actors.name: Other critics
actors.role: Nonresident defendants whose motions were not resolved here

proceedings: Plaintiffs sued four critics; Cole moved under Rule 12(b)(2).
District court dismissed as to Cole and declined transfer to Arizona.
limits: The order did not decide defamation merits or jurisdiction over all defendants. Other interviewees’ Michigan references were not Cole’s. The source’s transfer discussion changes statutory citations without explanation, while its denial is clear.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A participant’s mother criticizes an online organization
sections.cue: The interview and public posts reach a general audience
paragraphs: Jeffrey and Shaleia Ayan founded Twin Flames Universe, a Michigan corporation principally operating in Sutton Bay, offering spiritual guidance, relationship instruction, online courses, coaching, and a religious organization. They described roughly 10,000 members and hundreds of course hours intended to foster self-love and connection with a Twin Flame. Those claims were background, not judicial validation.

Louise Cole, an Arizona mother of a current participant, posted in 2019 on a public related subreddit, calling the organization a cult and multilevel marketing enterprise and expressing concern about family alienation. Other challenged criticism alleged manipulation, exploitation, and misconduct. These were disputed statements, not findings.

A Vancouver reporter interviewed Cole for a February 5, 2020 Vice article. She discussed her daughter’s work abroad, her own mistaken belief that classes involved Chinese medicine, payments, and lost communication. Other speakers described other experiences. The reporter called the Ayans Michigan YouTubers, and unnamed parents mentioned Michigan police; neither statement was attributed to Cole. She reposted the article.

sections.title: A cease-and-desist demand threatens the costs of Michigan litigation
paragraphs: In March 2020 plaintiffs demanded retractions and deletion and expressly threatened nonresident critics with travel, lodging, food, court, and lawyer costs in Michigan. A March 11 follow-up article described that letter; Cole declined to retract and said favorable member videos sounded scripted. Plaintiffs alleged at least four canceled contracts and sued four nonresident critics from Texas, Arizona, Florida, and Belgium for defamation, interference, and conspiracy.

Only Cole’s Rule 12(b)(2) motion was decided here, after March 3, 2021 argument. She said statements from Arizona to a Canadian journalist and worldwide readers did not target Michigan. Plaintiffs relied on knowledge, effects, and a suggestion that a Vancouver publication targeted nearby American consumers, including southeastern Michigan, because they had held Toronto workshops. Alternatively they requested Arizona transfer.

sections.title: Knowledge and local injury do not supply the defendant’s contacts
sections.cue: The court refuses to attribute other speakers’ targeting to Cole
paragraphs: Judge Gershwin Drain required reasonably particular prima facie facts on written submissions, favoring plaintiffs rather than accepting Cole’s conflicting account. Michigan’s long-arm reach was treated as coextensive with due process; its individual general-jurisdiction provision did not apply. Specific jurisdiction required purposeful forum conduct or consequences, a related claim, and a substantial reasonable connection.

Calder involved developed forum focus, sources, and circulation; Walden required the defendant’s connection rather than residence and injury supplied by plaintiffs. Sixth Circuit Blessing likewise did not treat social-media shaming of people with state ties as state-directed publication alone.

Plaintiffs offered no Michigan audience or circulation evidence for Vice and no explanation linking the Vancouver reporter specifically to southeastern Michigan. The article’s geographic statements belonged to other speakers. Cole’s public subreddit comments mentioned neither Michigan nor corporate location, and no Michigan followers or intended local readership were alleged. Business criticism did not necessarily aim at the business’s home state.

Michigan readers’ reactions and cancellations also were third-party choices, not Cole-created contacts. There was no prior Michigan relationship, transaction, or direct targeted communication. Even assuming she knew plaintiffs’ location, despite her disputed claim of learning it only through Vice, foreseeable injury there was insufficient.

sections.title: The threatening letter defeats the alternative transfer request
sections.cue: The ruling ends only Cole’s part of this forum dispute
paragraphs: Drain recognized interest-of-justice transfer despite missing jurisdiction, discussing §§ 1631 and 1406(a), though the application paragraph later referred to § 1404(a) without explanation. Ordinarily transfer could preserve a merits hearing after a forum mistake. Here the explicit threat to burden distant critics supported apparent bad faith in choosing Michigan. The suit was young, plaintiffs identified no prejudice from dismissal, and no limitations obstacle was suggested.

On March 23, 2021, the court granted Cole’s jurisdictional motion and declined transfer. It did not decide whether her statements were defamatory, resolve conspiracy merits, or dismiss every other defendant on the same record.
